跟着中国留学生チェン，从落地机场到毕业致辞，学会区役所、租房、医院、入管等真实场: Follow Chen, an international student from China, from the moment he lands at the airport to his graduation speech, and learn natural Japanese for real-life situations like the ward office, renting an apartment, the hospital, and the immigration office.
到达机场入境: Arriving at the airport and going through immigration
四月初的傍晚，チェン坐了四个小时飞机降落在成田机场。他排在外国人入境审查的队伍里: It's early evening at the beginning of April. After a four-hour flight, Chen has just landed at Narita Airport. He's standing in the immigration line for foreign nationals, and his palms won't stop sweating. Once he's through immigration and has his residence card, the person waiting for him in the arrivals lobby is Sakura, a Japanese friend he met earlier on a language exchange website.
成田机场的入境审查官，四十多岁，语速慢、公事公办: Immigration officer at Narita Airport, in his forties; speaks slowly and is strictly businesslike
中国留学生，二十岁，经济学部一年级，刚到日本，认真但容易紧张: International student from China, 20 years old, first-year student in the Faculty of Economics; just arrived in Japan; conscientious but gets nervous easily
日本大学生，和チェン同一所大学，网上语言交换认识了半年，开朗热心: Japanese university student at the same university as Chen; they've known each other for six months through an online language exchange; cheerful and warmhearted
审查官和旅客是完全陌生的公务关系，对方用简单的丁宁语提问，チェン只要用「です・ま: The immigration officer and the traveler are complete strangers in an official relationship. The officer asks questions in simple polite Japanese, and all Chen needs to do is answer briefly with 「です・ます」; there's no need for honorific language. Sakura and Chen have already been chatting online in the plain (casual) style for six months, so naturally they use the plain style when they meet in person too. That's why, within a single lesson, the tone suddenly shifts from "official business" to "friends."
你好。请出示护照和入境卡。: Hello. Please show me your passport and arrival card.
递东西的时候说一句「お願いします」就很得体，相当于“麻烦您看一下”。不用说「どう: When you hand something over, just saying 「お願いします」 is perfectly appropriate; it's like saying "please take a look." Don't say 「どうぞ」: 「どうぞ」 is a bit like "go ahead" or "here, take it," and saying it to an immigration officer sounds too casual. If you open your passport to the photo page and hand it over with both hands, the officer will see you as cooperative.
你来日本做什么？: What have you come to Japan to do?
留学。我在东京的大学学习。: Study abroad. I'll be studying at a university in Tokyo.
审查时回答越短越清楚越好。先用一个词「留学です」回答核心，再补一句具体内容。不要: At immigration, the shorter and clearer your answers, the better. First answer the core question in a word, 「留学です」, then add one sentence of detail. Don't use long sentences just to show off your Japanese. The officer deals with hundreds of people every day, and what they want most is an answer they can understand the moment they hear it.
你在日本待多久？: How long will you be in Japan?
「四年」读「よねん」，不读「しねん」。数字的读法在窗口办事时经常被问到，四（よ・: 「四年」 is read 「よねん」, not 「しねん」. You'll often be asked about numbers at service counters, so make sure you've practiced the readings of 「四」 (よ, よん), 「七」 (なな), and 「九」 (きゅう) until they're second nature.
住的地方定下来了吗？: Have you decided where you'll be living?
定了，是大学的宿舍。我写在卡上了。: Yes, in the university dormitory. I wrote it on the card.
那么，请把两只手的食指放在这里。接下来请看摄像头。: Now, please place both index fingers here. Next, please look at the camera.
好了。这是你的在留卡。住址定下来以后，请在十四天之内到区役所登记。: All right, you're all set. This is your residence card. Once your address is settled, please report it to the ward office within 14 days.
这里的「結構です」是“可以了、没问题了”的意思，不是拒绝。同一个词在别的场合（比: Here, 「結構です」 means "that's fine, you're all set"; it isn't a refusal. In other situations (for example, when someone offers you something), the same 「結構です」 means "no, thank you," so you have to judge from the tone and the situation.
明白了。谢谢您。: I understand. Thank you very much.
啊，さくら！谢谢你来接我。: Oh, Sakura! Thanks for coming to pick me up.
「〜てくれて、ありがとう」是在感谢“对方为我做的那件事”，比只说「ありがとう」具: 「〜てくれて、ありがとう」 thanks the other person for "the thing they did for me," which is much more specific than just saying 「ありがとう」. Japanese people care a lot about whether you've noticed the time and effort they've put in. Putting what they did into words is a way of saying "I see the trouble you went to."
没事。长途旅行辛苦了。累了吧？: Not at all. It's been a long trip for you. You must be tired, right?
嗯，有一点。其实我过入境审查的时候太紧张，声音都在抖。: Yeah, a little. Actually, I got so nervous at immigration that my voice was shaking.
没关系，一开始大家都这样。走吧！: Don't worry, everyone's like that at first. Okay, let's go!
「入国審査を受ける」= 接受入境审查；机场指示牌上写的是这个词: 「入国審査を受ける」 = to go through immigration; this is the word written on the signs at the airport
「パスポートを見せる」= 出示护照，窗口办事时常和在留卡一起要求出示: 「パスポートを見せる」 = to show one's passport; at service counters you'll often be asked to show it along with your residence card
中长期居留外国人的身份证，必须随身携带；成田、羽田、关西等机场入境时当场发放: The ID card for foreign nationals living in Japan on a mid- to long-term basis, which must be carried at all times; it's issued on the spot when you enter Japan at airports such as Narita, Haneda, and Kansai
「留学に来る」「留学生」；签证（在留资格）的名称也叫「留学」: 「留学に来る」 (to come to study abroad), 「留学生」 (international student); the visa (status of residence) is also called 「留学」
「大学の寮」「学生寮」；公司宿舍叫「社員寮」: 「大学の寮」 (university dormitory), 「学生寮」 (student dormitory); a company dormitory is called 「社員寮」
入境时按指纹用；「親指」是大拇指: Used for fingerprinting when you enter Japan; 「親指」 is the thumb
审查官说是“可以了”；别人推荐东西时说是委婉的“不用了”，要看场合: From an immigration officer, it means "that's fine"; said when someone offers you something, it's a polite "no, thank you"; it depends on the situation
「住所が決まる」= 住址定下来；所有手续都会问: 「住所が決まる」 = to have one's address settled; you'll be asked for it in every procedure
「十四日以内」「三十分以内」；表示期限，办手续时一定要听清: 「十四日以内」 (within 14 days), 「三十分以内」 (within 30 minutes); it indicates a deadline, so listen carefully for it when doing paperwork
东京等大城市叫区役所，其他地方叫「市役所」「町役場」；住民登记在这里办: In Tokyo and other big cities it's called 「区役所」; elsewhere it's 「市役所」 (city hall) or 「町役場」 (town office); resident registration is done here
「区役所に届ける」= 向区役所申报；「荷物を届ける」= 送东西: 「区役所に届ける」 = to report (something) to the ward office; 「荷物を届ける」 = to deliver a package
「迎えに来る」= 来接；「迎えに行く」= 去接: 「迎えに来る」 = to come to pick (someone) up; 「迎えに行く」 = to go to pick (someone) up
常用「長旅、お疲れさま」慰劳刚到的人: Often used in 「長旅、お疲れさま」 to acknowledge the effort of someone who has just arrived
「緊張して声が震える」；说出来反而会让对方想帮你: 「緊張して声が震える」 (to be so nervous your voice shakes); saying it out loud actually makes people want to help you
动词ます形去ます + に来る，或 名词（勉強・観光）+ をしに来る: Verb ます-stem (drop ます) + に来る, or noun (勉強・観光) + をしに来る
表示“来的目的”。审查官、新邻居、打工的店长都可能这样问你。回答时不一定要重复整: Expresses "the purpose of coming." Immigration officers, new neighbors, and the manager at your part-time job might all ask you this. When answering, you don't have to repeat the whole sentence; 「留学です」 or 「観光です」 is enough. In casual conversation, saying 「日本の文化を勉強しに来ました」 will make people want to get to know you better.
我来接朋友。: I came to pick up a friend.
「住所が決まったら」是“等住址定下来以后”，说的是一件一定会发生的事，之后要做什: 「住所が決まったら」 means "once your address is settled": it talks about something that will definitely happen and what to do after it. Staff at service counters often use 「〜たら、〜てください」 to tell you the next step, so when you hear 「たら」, prick up your ears: what comes next is your next task.
住址定了以后，请去区役所。: Once your address is settled, please go to the ward office.
到了以后联系我哦。: Let me know when you get there, okay?
谢谢你为我……: thank you for doing ... for me
动词て形 + くれて、ありがとう（礼貌：〜てくださって、ありがとうございます）: Verb て-form + 「くれて、ありがとう」 (polite: 「〜てくださって、ありがとうございます」)
把对方为你做的事说出来再道谢，对方会感到自己的用心被看见了。对朋友用「〜てくれて: When you put into words what the other person did for you before thanking them, they feel that their effort has been noticed. Use 「〜てくれて、ありがとう」 with friends and 「〜てくださって、ありがとうございます」 with teachers and older people. Just saying 「ありがとう」 isn't wrong, but it lacks warmth.
谢谢你来接我。: Thanks for coming to pick me up.
谢谢您告诉我。: Thank you very much for telling me.
入境审查、海关、窗口办事时，用最简单的「です・ます」回答，短句、名词先行，例如「: At immigration, customs, or a service counter, answer in the simplest 「です・ます」 form, with short sentences that lead with the key noun, such as 「留学です」 and 「四年です」. When you meet a friend who's come to pick you up, start by thanking them for making the trip.
不要为了显得日语好而讲长句或者开玩笑，审查官不需要寒暄。也不要用普通体回答「うん: Don't use long sentences or crack jokes to show off your Japanese; immigration officers don't need small talk. Don't answer in the plain style, like 「うん、留学」, either. And don't assume that 「結構です」 always means a refusal. If you don't understand, just say 「すみません、もう一度お願いします」.
审查官看到你简短、清楚、配合，就会觉得“这个人没问题”，审查很快结束。さくら听到: When the officer sees that you're brief, clear, and cooperative, they'll think "this person is fine," and the inspection will be over quickly. When Sakura hears "thanks for coming to pick me up," she'll feel that waiting an hour at the airport was worth it, and she'll be even more willing to help you in the future.
很多人第一次过日本的入境审查都会紧张，这很正常。审查官表情严肃，不是因为讨厌你，: Lots of people get nervous the first time they go through immigration in Japan, and that's perfectly normal. The officer looks stern not because they dislike you, but because they have to carefully check hundreds of passports every day, and a single oversight could lead to serious trouble. Once you appreciate how demanding their job is, you'll know the best way to cooperate: open your passport to the photo page, answer exactly what you're asked, and place your fingers straight when giving your fingerprints. In the arrivals lobby, Chen admits to Sakura that he was so nervous his voice shook, and there's nothing embarrassing about that. In Japan, people who are willing to say out loud that they feel anxious actually find it easier to get help. When Sakura says "everyone's like that at first," she's giving you a push forward. Don't be afraid: you've already taken the first step.
入境审查官问「日本へは何をしに来ましたか」，最合适的回答是？: The immigration officer asks 「日本へは何をしに来ましたか」. What's the most appropriate answer?
审查时用「です」简短回答目的即可。「うん」是普通体，太随便；表达热情或含糊其辞都: At immigration, a brief answer stating your purpose with 「です」 is all you need. 「うん」 is plain style and too casual, and gushing with enthusiasm or giving a vague answer will both make the officer ask more questions.
审查官把在留卡交给你时说「はい、結構です」，意思是？: When the immigration officer hands you your residence card and says 「はい、結構です」, what does it mean?
可以了，手续完成: That's fine, the procedure is complete
很好，你的日语不错: Very good, your Japanese is great
这里的「結構です」表示“没问题、可以了”。只有在对方推荐或给你东西时，「結構です: Here, 「結構です」 means "no problem, that's fine." 「結構です」 means "no, thank you" only when someone is offering or giving you something.
さくら专门来机场接你，下面哪句最能让她感到被感谢？: Sakura came all the way to the airport to pick you up. Which of the following would best make her feel appreciated?
「〜てくれて、ありがとう」把对方做的事说了出来，而且是朋友之间的普通体。「ありが: 「〜てくれて、ありがとう」 puts what she did into words, and it's in the plain style used between friends. 「ありがとうございました」 is too polite for a friend and sounds distant.
